title: Baca County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Baca County the median well depth is 270 ft and most wells make over 172.5 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply.
h1: Water wells in Baca County, Colorado
intro_html:
If you’re looking at land or a home on a well anywhere in Baca County, the state’s well records give a pretty clear picture. Depths, yields, and water levels here are driven by plains sediment, big irrigation wells in the Ogallala and Southern High Plains aquifers, and some fractured-bedrock wells.

Below is what those numbers mean in practical terms for drilling costs, water supply, and risk if you’re buying or planning to build near places like Springfield, Walsh, Two Buttes, Vilas, Pritchett, or Campo.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Baca County
sections.html:
Across Baca County, the median well depth is 270 feet, with the middle half between 175 and 392 feet. About 46% of wells fall in the 100–300 foot range, and another 41% run 300–600 feet. Only 9% are under 100 feet, and a small share, 4%, go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record hits 4,249 feet, which tells you how far some irrigation or problem wells have had to chase water.

On an individual parcel near Springfield, Walsh, Two Buttes, Vilas, Pritchett, or Campo, I’d plan bids around that 175–392 foot band unless nearby logs show otherwise. Plains alluvium and sedimentary rock generally drill easier than mountain granite, but depth variability is still real, especially moving between Ogallala, Southern High Plains, and fractured-bedrock settings.

sections.heading: Drilling and completion cost expectations here
sections.html:
In Baca County’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, current drilling runs roughly $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 270 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself around $9,400–$14,800. By the time you add steel or PVC casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and basic electrical, a finished domestic well typically lands in the $15,400–$26,800 range at that depth.

Deeper wells toward the 392-foot upper-middle range scale quickly with footage. When you compare lots in Springfield, Walsh, Pritchett, or Campo, pay attention to nearby well depths in the state database. A 200-foot neighborhood versus a 400-foot one can mean many thousands of dollars difference on a new build, even before the house goes up.

sections.heading: Well yields: strong irrigation capacity, plenty for homes
sections.html:
Of the wells that report production, the median yield in Baca County is a very strong 650 gpm, with the middle half between 172.5 and 1000 gpm. About 89% of reported wells make more than 15 gpm, and only 1% come in under 1 gpm, with another 1% in the 1–5 gpm band.

That big capacity lines up with the use mix: roughly 54% of permits are for irrigation and 27% for stock, which often means large Ogallala or Southern High Plains wells. Domestic and household wells are about 12% of the total. For a single home, even 5–10 gpm is usually workable under Colorado’s household-use rules, so these numbers suggest plenty of water when sited correctly. Still, always look at domestic wells near your parcel, not just the big pivot wells.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the aquifer
sections.html:
Only 212 Baca County wells report a static water level, but they show a median depth to water of about 134 feet, with the middle half between 43 and 195 feet. That’s the water level in the casing before pumping, not the total well depth.

By decade, median water levels were about 76 feet below surface in the 1950s, 90 in the 1960s, 64 in the 1970s, about 80 in the 2010s, then dropped to around 180 feet in the 2020s. That recent jump deeper suggests a declining water table in parts of the county, likely tied to long-term irrigation pumping in the Ogallala and Southern High Plains aquifers. When you review a specific lot, check nearby well logs for both depth and static level, not just yield.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and how activity has changed
sections.html:
Baca County has 5,376 wells in the state records, with 1,783 listed as constructed and 3,198 giving a total depth. The busiest drilling decades were the 1960s with about 955 permits and the 1970s with about 782. Activity dipped in the 1980s, then picked back up with 587 permits in the 2000s and 563 in the 2010s. There are already 274 permits in the 2020s, with records current through 2025.

Most active drillers on record include Ralph'S Welding (Woods, Ralph R) with 226 wells, Hegwood Drilling (Hegwood, Spencer) with 201, and Konkel Drilling (Konkel, David Leroy) with 132. When you evaluate a lot, it’s worth pulling the specific driller and construction details from nearby wells for a sense of how they were built.

sections.heading: Risks to check: quality, low-yield pockets, and siting
sections.html:
The county’s high median yield of 650 gpm and the fact that only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm look good on paper, but that doesn’t remove local risk. Around your tract, there can still be thin or tight zones in fractured bedrock or margins of the Ogallala that don’t perform like the big irrigation wells.

On the quality side, there are 18 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and about 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations within roughly 10 miles in the county. That doesn’t mean your water is bad, but it’s a clear signal to test a new or existing well. Also plan good separation between wells and septic systems when you lay out a new build so you don’t create your own contamination issue.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Baca County
sections.html:
For a parcel near Springfield, Walsh, Two Buttes, Vilas, Pritchett, or Campo, start by pulling nearby well permits and note three things: depth (often in that 175–392 foot band), yield, and static water level. Remember that many of the county’s 54% irrigation and 27% stock wells are oversized compared with a domestic well and may tap a different part of the aquifer.

If you’re planning a new house, ask your designer and driller to coordinate well and septic locations early. Colorado exempt household wells are typically limited in use even when the aquifer could produce far more than the 35 gpm pumping limit, so build your water plan around the well permit conditions, not just what nearby irrigation wells can do.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Baca County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Baca County the median well depth is about 270 feet, with the middle half of wells between 175 and 392 feet. Roughly 46% of wells are 100–300 feet deep and about 41% are 300–600 feet. Only about 9% are shallower than 100 feet. A few irrigation and problem wells go far deeper, with the deepest recorded well reaching 4,249 feet.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Baca County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported yields in Baca County are strong. The median well produces about 650 gpm, and the middle half fall between 172.5 and 1000 gpm. Around 89% of wells with data make more than 15 gpm, while only about 1% report under 1 gpm and another 1% are in the 1–5 gpm range. That’s more than enough for a typical household well when permitted correctly.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Baca County, Colorado?
faq.a: With alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, drilling in Baca County typically runs about $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 270 feet, the drilled hole alone comes out around $9,400–$14,800. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and basic electrical usually totals about $15,400–$26,800 at that depth, not counting any unusual site work or power upgrades.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Baca County, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level records are limited, but they show a recent deepening. Median depth to water was about 76–90 feet in the 1950s–1960s, around 64 feet in the 1970s, roughly 80 feet in the 2010s, and then about 180 feet in the 2020s. That jump deeper in the 2020s suggests a declining water table in parts of the county, likely related to long-term irrigation pumping.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Baca County, Colorado?
faq.a: The state well records don’t rate potability, but they do show potential concerns: there are about 18 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations within roughly 10 miles. Many homes still rely on wells, but you should plan on a full lab test for any existing or new well before using it for drinking, and then follow up with treatment if needed.
